While this kinetic process occurs at scales of order the cosmic ray gyroradius, many orders of magnitude below the current resolution limit of galaxy evolution simulations, fluid theories of this streaming transport have been developed and, with the advent of various numerical techniques, implemented in MHD codes for use in a galaxy-scale context. With these tools now available, our understanding of cosmic ray influence in the interstellar, circumgalactic, and intracluster medium has rapidly progressed; however, as of this writing, two important trends are evident in most published simulations: 1) it's assumed that GeV-energy cosmic ray transport proceeds as if the background thermal gas is everywhere fully ionized. In reality, the waves the cosmic rays resonate with propagate only in the ions, and streaming is therefore at the ion Alfvén speed $v_A^{ion} = v_A/\sqrt{f_{ion}}$. Also, ion-neutral friction can damp the confining waves, thereby decoupling cosmic rays and greatly increasing their diffusive flux; 2) partially neutral ISM clouds and other density irregularities that induce decoupling and nonlinear cosmic transport are frequently under-resolved. If we imagine the multiphase ISM as an obstacle course of coupled vs decoupled regimes, further complicated by hadronic and Coulomb collisions between cosmic rays and ambient gas, then how do cosmic rays navigate this medium, and can we constrain this transport with observations? The answers have implications for ISM dynamics, interpretation of observations, and the acceleration of cold interstellar gas in galactic winds and fountains. In this paper, we presented a suite of high-resolution, idealized simulations of cosmic ray fronts navigating the multiphase ISM. We ran each simulation twice: first, assuming the medium is fully ionized and, second, accounting for changes in ionization that induce “ionization-dependent transport”. We began with 1D simulations of an energetically significant cosmic ray front hitting a single, partially neutral cloud with radius and density typical of ISM conditions. We then explored how cosmic ray transport, cosmic ray energy loss, and cloud acceleration and morphology varied in multiple dimensions and varying magnetic field strength. We then ran the same cosmic ray fronts through mock ISM setups: slabs of lognormally-distributed multiphase clumps on top of an exponentially decaying mean density. We assessed how cosmic rays sampled the ISM and how ionization-dependent transport affected cloud acceleration and collisional and collisionless energy loss. Our main findings were: * Cloud interfaces can play a crucial role in setting the cosmic ray propagation through the cloud interior. The drop in Alfvén speed while the gas is still fully ionized leads to a bottleneck in the interface; this reinforces the cosmic ray pressure gradient that generates confining waves and locks cosmic rays to the wave frame. The effects of ion-neutral damping are thereby suppressed, and the advective flux rather than diffusive flux generally dominates transport ($v_{st} \approx v_A^{ion}$). * The stair-step structure that develops at cloud interfaces facilitates collisionless energy transfer from the cosmic rays to waves $\propto v_A^{ion} \nabla P_{CR}$. Unlike for a fully ionized cloud where a single cosmic ray gradient forms (Wiener et al. 2017a, 2019), there's now a bottleneck at both the front *and* back cloud edges. In our mock ISM simulations, this extra energy loss partially offsets a reduction in collisional energy loss, keeping the total cosmic ray calorimetry similar to when full ionization is assumed. The additional gas heating may also have implications for ion abundances and kinematics at cloud interfaces, though we estimate that the role of heating would be secondary to cooling and conduction. We plan to explore this further by more self-consistently modeling interface properties rather than leaving the interface width as a free parameter. * Cosmic rays sample the ISM differently when varying ionization is accounted for. Ionization-dependent transport allows cosmic rays to leak into dense cloud interiors while, assuming full ionization, cosmic rays are confined to thin cloud boundary layers. These differences are imprinted on gamma-ray emission maps. * Total collisional losses are very similar for the two transport models. With ionization-dependent transport, short cosmic ray residence times in clouds are offset by the denser gas they access. So while gamma-ray emission maps with the two transport models look very different, the gamma-ray luminosity is dominantly set by the cosmic ray transport in the warm ionized medium, which is the same in each transport model. This result is consistent with Hopkins et al. (2020b). * When ionization is accounted for, cloud acceleration is decreased since ionization-dependent transport in cloud interiors flattens the cosmic ray pressure profile. The change is not as large as one might expect, however, as our simulations exhibit a factor < 2 difference in cold gas momentum. Cosmic rays still bottleneck at the cloud edges, leading to pressure gradient forces that push the <!-- page 27 -->
cloud. This suggests that, contrary to previous expectation, ionization-dependent transport does not greatly inhibit cosmic rays from accelerating cold, molecular gas in galactic outflows. The magnetic field topology, which can be warped upstream by strong cosmic ray fronts, may be a greater inhibitor of direct cosmic ray acceleration of clouds. We will explore these aspects more thoroughly in a future study. Clearly, cosmic ray propagation through the multi-phase ISM is a very rich problem with fundamental implications for ISM dynamics and feedback. To understand how cosmic rays shape their environments, we need to continue applying first-principle cosmic ray transport models to astrophysical problems, test the outcomes against observations, and use those constraints to create more complete models of cosmic ray transport. Simulations that employ streaming at the gas Alfvén speed will drastically underestimate transport speeds in partially neutral clouds, thereby overestimating cloud acceleration. On the other hand, constant field-aligned diffusion models have no dependence on local gas conditions, thereby precluding bottleneck formation at cloud interfaces, and they omit the energy transfer from cosmic rays to thermal gas, fundamentally changing cosmic ray influence on galaxies (Wiener et al. 2017b). “Two-κ” prescriptions (e.g. Farber et al. 2018), while tying the transport speed to local gas temperature, again prohibit bottlenecks at cloud interfaces and may overestimate the effective transport speed depending on the choice of $κ$. These models, then, likely underestimate the dynamical influence of cosmic rays on partially neutral gas. In light of our results, we instead advocate that galaxy evolution simulations should, to zeroth order, model streaming at the ion Alfvén speed with a temperature-based ion fraction. This method will more fully capture the generation of bottlenecks and steep pressure gradients at cloud interfaces, as well as ionization-dependent transport in cloud interiors that is robust, at least in these simulations, to changes in ionization fraction. More detailed modeling of ionization from local sources and lower energy cosmic rays could alter this picture and should be a next step. # APPENDIX ## 1. *Effect of Resolution* In this section, we carry out a small resolution study, primarily in 1D, to test convergence and inform larger-scale simulations of galaxy evolution, which may under-resolve cosmic ray interactions with multiphase structures. # THE LONGITUDINAL TRANSPORT OF ENERGETIC IONS FROM IMPULSIVE SOLAR FLARES IN INTERPLANETARY SPACE J. GIACALONE AND J. R. JOKIPII Department of Planetary Sciences, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA
*Received 2011 December 29; accepted 2012 May 1; published 2012 May 14* ## ABSTRACT We present a study of the longitudinal spread of energetic charged particles from a localized instantaneous compact source on the Sun. Our study utilizes a diffusive-transport model for the propagation of energetic ions in interplanetary space. We show that even for very small values of the ratio of perpendicular to parallel diffusion coefficients—a few percent—the particles spread significantly in longitude. Spatial diffusion and adiabatic energy loss of ions in the interplanetary plasma cause impulsive particle events at Earth's orbit to last a few days. In this time, the combination of transport both along and across the local Parker-spiral magnetic field and the longitudinal motion of the magnetic lines of forces rooted at the Sun as it rotates leads to substantial longitudinal transport of the particles. We show that spacecraft separated by as much as 180° or more may observe events associated with compact solar sources, such as those from impulsive solar flares. Our results are qualitatively consistent with recent multi-spacecraft observations. *Key words:* diffusion – scattering – Sun: flares – Sun: heliosphere ## 1. INTRODUCTION Understanding solar-energetic particles (SEPs) involves both the physics of particle acceleration at the Sun and charged-particle transport from the acceleration site to an observer. This Letter addresses the latter. The transport of SEPs in interplanetary space involves several effects, including pitch-angle scattering in the turbulent interplanetary magnetic field (IMF), drifts in the large-scale magnetic field, energy change in the expanding solar wind, and cross-field diffusion. Cross-field diffusion results from particles moving off of magnetic lines of force due to drifts and/or scattering, and by following field lines that meander relative to the average magnetic field (e.g., Jokipii 1966; Jokipii & Parker 1969; Forman et al. 1974; Bieber & Matthaeus 1997). For the case of SEPs with energies below about 1 GeV, cross-field transport results primarily from the particles following meandering magnetic lines of force (Giacalone & Jokipii 1999). A particularly useful class of SEP events for studying the physics of interplanetary transport of charged particles are those associated with impulsive solar flares. It is thought that such events are well represented as an impulsive release of energetic particles at a compact source. Such events are typically identified at 1 AU by both their composition and their time-intensity profile (Reames et al. 1999). These are characterized by unusually large enhancements of $^3\text{He}^{++}$ relative to $^4\text{He}^{++}$ (Hsieh & Simpson 1970; Reames et al. 1994), are rich in electrons, and are usually short lived, typically lasting a few days. By associating in situ particle events observed at 1 AU with solar flares, Reames et al. (1999) noted the flares are narrowly confined to the western limb of the solar disk. This is presumably because the particles tend to follow closely the Parker spiral magnetic field whose lines of force connect with near-Earth spacecraft. Wibberenz & Cane (2006) used three-spacecraft observations of energetic electrons associated with impulsive solar flares to study this further. They found that in many events, the longitudinal spread is significantly larger than expected. Pei (2007) solved the cosmic-ray transport equation for test electrons moving in a large-scale turbulent IMF showing a reasonable agreement with these observations for values of the perpendicular to parallel diffusion coefficient of about 10%–25%. Recently, three spacecraft—STEREO A and B and ACE—observed energetic ions characteristic of impulsive SEP events that appeared to be from the same compact source at the Sun (ACE news item 137). At the time of the observation, the spacecraft were separated by about 130° in heliolongitude. If the events observed came from the same source, this implies a somewhat larger longitudinal transport of energetic ions than has been observed previously. It is interesting to note that there are other observations that suggest there is little cross-field transport of impulsive SEPs. Mazur et al. (2000) noted that many of these events show intermittent intensity depletions, or “dropouts,” during the event. The existence of dropouts suggest that charged particles adhere closely to magnetic lines of force, hence the abrupt depletion of particles at all energies (Chollet & Giacalone 2011). The intermittent nature of dropouts is likely the result of field-line meandering, leading to the mixing of field lines that connect to the flare source with those that don’t (Giacalone et al. 2000). A similar, but somewhat different interpretation of the dropout phenomenon is given by Chuychai et al. (2007). This Letter studies the transport of SEPs associated with impulsive solar flares focusing particularly on their transport in heliolongitude. Our work is similar to that of Droge et al. (2012), with a key difference being our emphasis on the longitudinal particle transport used to understand recent observations made by spacecraft widely separated in longitude. ## 2. NUMERICAL MODEL We utilize the diffusive-transport model for SEPs—the well-known cosmic-ray transport equation of Parker (1965). This equation is valid when the pitch-angle distribution is nearly isotropic. It is well known that the earliest arriving particles in most SEP events are highly anisotropic, moving along the magnetic field, but that later in the event the distributions are more isotropic. Our primary goal is to obtain reasonable estimates of the expected longitudinal distribution of the event-integrated intensity of SEPs from compact solar sources. Thus, while our approach does not consider pitch-angle anisotropies of the earliest arriving particles, it is appropriate for studying the entire event which, for ions, can last a few days. <!-- page 2 -->
Our model assumes a two-dimensional spherical geometry with latitudinal symmetry. Thus, we neglect latitudinal diffusion and any variations of the SEP distribution with latitude. This assumption is reasonable for SEP events that remain relatively confined in latitude. Since the transport of charged particles across the magnetic field is considerably smaller than that along the field (e.g., Giacalone & Jokipii 1999), and since the average magnetic field—the Parker spiral—does not have a latitudinal component, the particles are not expected to diffuse significantly in latitude for events lasting a few days. Note that longitudinal transport can be large since the particles move along the Parker-spiral magnetic field which has a significant longitudinal component. The general form for the Parker transport equation has been written down many times and is not repeated here (cf. Jokipii 1971; Giacalone 2010). The spatial diffusion tensor, $\kappa_{i,j}$, can be separated into components along ($\kappa_{\parallel}$) and across ($\kappa_{\perp}$) the magnetic field according to $$
\kappa_{i,j} = \kappa_{\perp} \delta_{i,j} + (\kappa_{\parallel} - \kappa_{\perp}) \frac{B_i B_j}{B^2}, \quad (1)
$$ where $\delta_{i,j}$ is the Kronicker delta, $B_i$ is the magnetic field vector, and $B$ is its magnitude. Here we neglect the antisymmetric component, $\kappa_A$, which leads to particle drifts. It can be shown that for our assumed geometry $\kappa_A$ has no effect. For our application, we assume the solar wind moves radially outward from the Sun at a constant speed $V_w$, and assume the magnetic field is given by $$
B_i = \mathbf{B} = B_0 \left(\frac{R_0}{r}\right)^2 \left(\hat{r} - \frac{r\Omega_\odot}{V_w}\hat{\phi}\right), \quad (2)
$$ where $R_0$ is the source surface and $\Omega_\odot$ is the solar rotation frequency. We note that this has the form of the usual Parker spiral magnetic field only in the solar-equatorial plane since, in our problem, there is no latitudinal dependence. For all simulations presented in this Letter, we take $V_w = 4 \times 10^7 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, $B_0 = 1.6 \text{ G}$, and $R_0 = R_\odot = 6.96 \times 10^{10} \text{ cm}$. We solve Parker's transport equation using stochastic integration in which a large number of individual elements of the distribution $f$, or “pseudoparticles,” are advanced in time according to $$
r_{n+1} = r_n + \xi_1 \sqrt{2\kappa_{\perp}\Delta t} + \xi_3 \sqrt{2(\kappa_{\parallel} - \kappa_{\perp})\Delta t} \left(\frac{B_r}{B}\right) + \left[\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} (r^2 \kappa_{rr}) + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \kappa_{r\phi}}{\partial \phi} + V_w\right] \Delta t \quad (3)
$$ $$
\phi_{n+1} = \phi_n + \frac{1}{r} \left( \xi_2 \sqrt{2\kappa_{\perp}\Delta t} + \xi_3 \sqrt{2(\kappa_{\parallel} - \kappa_{\perp})\Delta t} \frac{B_{\phi}}{B} \right) + \left[ \frac{\partial \kappa_{r\phi}}{\partial r} + \frac{\kappa_{r\phi}}{r} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \kappa_{\phi\phi}}{\partial \phi} \right] \Delta t \quad (4)
$$ $$
p_{n+1} = p_n \left( 1 - \frac{\Delta t}{3} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{U} \right), \quad (5)
$$ where $r_n$ and $\phi_n$ represent the position of each pseudoparticle at time $t_n = n\Delta t$, where $\Delta t$ (=5 s in all simulations) is the time step. All quantities on the right of Equations (3)–(5) are evaluated at time $t_n$. The quantities $\xi_1$, $\xi_2$, and $\xi_3$ are zero-mean, unit variance random variables.

Scientific Background ### 2.1. Jovian Electrons as Test Particles The scientific discussion of Jovian electrons dates back to the early 1970s when McDonald et al. (1972) proposed the existence of a dominant Jovian source by addressing the correlation of the ~ 13 month periodicity in low-MeV electron counting rate measurements at Earth orbit with Jupiter's synodic period. After the Jupiter flyby of *Pioneer 10*, Teegarden et al. (1974) were able to confirm this hypothesis based on data obtained by the Charged Particle Instrument (CPI). Pyle & Simpson (1977) showed, by analysing the electron fluxes as function of distance and their dependence on the occurrence of Corotating Interaction Regions (CIRs), that the Jovian source is not only quasi-continuous but also point-like. This refers to the observation that no electron emission could be detected from Jupiter's magnetotail which extends up to over 1 AU into the heliosphere. As the dominant particle population from a few to several tens of MeV in the inner heliosphere, Jovian electrons soon became the subject of charged particle transport modelling (Conlon 1978; Zhang et al. 2017). Due to Jupiter's decentral position, the magnetic connection by means of the Parker spirals determines whether the electrons reach the observer primarily via motion along the field or by diffusion perpendicular to it. Thus, Jovian electrons are ideal candidates to probe the electron diffusion coefficients in the inner heliosphere. Jovian electrons were used as test particles to model the charged-particle transport computationally (see e. g. Chenette et al. 1977; Conlon 1978; Fichtner et al. 2000; Zhang et al. 2007, and references therein) to ascertain the diffusion coefficients parallel and perpendicular to the Heliospheric Magnetic Field (HMF). This was usually done by comparing computed with measured electron intensities at Earth during periods of good/bad magnetic connection. Furthermore, given the demonstrated sensitivity of computed low-energy galactic electron intensities to various turbulence quantities (see Engelbrecht & Burger 2010, 2013; Engelbrecht 2019), it may be possible to draw conclusions from Jovian electrons as to the behaviour of those quantities in regions of the heliosphere where spacecraft observations of the samedo not exist (see, e.g., Engelbrecht 2017). Since these transport parameters and the diffusion coefficients depend on are highly spatially dependent, the time that particles reside in a certain part of the heliosphere may yield significant insights to the modulation of GCRs as well. Florinski & Pogorelov (2009) showed this dependency for GCR protons, investigating the time they spend in the heliotail, the heliosheath and in the solar wind within the termination shock, respectively. Utilizing both galactic electrons and protons, Strauss et al. (2011b) focused on the connection between the total propagation time and energy losses. They find a significant non-linear dependency on the total propagation times, which is strong enough to influence also the observations of Jovian electrons. These energy losses are entirely caused by adiabatic effects as other possible influences such as particle-particle interactions are negligible in the TPE due to a lack of significance in the interplanetary medium. As the adiabatic energy changes $dE/dt \sim -2/3 \cdot E_{SW}/r$ are connected to the radial position, the corresponding energy loss rate per step only depend on the temporal step size $\Delta s$ and the radial position after the step. The radial direction of the step thereby is irrelevant. This leads to particles spending more simulation time at small radii losing more energy and implicitly to a statistical connection between the average energy losses and the particle's mean free paths. ### 2.2. The Jovian Electron Spectrum Parallel to the efforts of studying Jovian electron transport, the Jovian source itself has been investigated intensively. The main unknowns are the energy spectrum of the source and how the particles are accelerated. **Source energy spectrum:** Although widely considered to be dominant in its energy range, the shape and exact strength of the Jovian source remains a topic of debate. A first suggestion was published as soon as *Pioneer 10* confirmed the existence of the source by Teegarden et al. (1974), but the limited amount of flyby data and the general difficulties inherent to measuring electrons, especially electron spectra, made it difficult to further constrain both the magnitude and the shape.

### III. METHODOLOGY #### A. The stochastic method Our calculations are based on the so-called stochastic differential equation (SDE) method. It consists in transforming the Parker equation into a set of SDEs that can be integrated using Monte-Carlo techniques. The solution of Eq. 1 is then obtained by sampling. The SDE method is implemented in several solar modulation codes and in the recent years, with the increase of computing power and resources, is has become very popular [8, 17, 25, 27, 37, 64, 67]. A nice review on this subject is provided in Strauss & Effenberger [46]. For a stochastic process, the stochastic equation can be recast in the form: $$
\delta \vec{r} = (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{K}^{\mathbf{S}} - \vec{V}) \delta t + \mathbf{S} \cdot \delta \vec{W}, \quad (8)
$$ where $\vec{V} = \vec{V}_{sw} + \langle \vec{V}_d \rangle$ is the total velocity of the particle, $\mathbf{S}$ is a matrix such that $\mathbf{S} \cdot \mathbf{S} = 2\mathbf{K}^{\mathbf{S}}$, and $\delta \vec{W}$ is a multidimensional Wiener process related to a normalized gaussian distribution. The corresponding change of kinetic energy $E$ in the time $\delta t$, for a CR proton with mass $m_p$ is given by: $$
\delta E = \left( \frac{2V_{sw}}{3r} \right) \frac{E^2 + 2m_p E}{E + m_p} \delta t \quad (9)
$$ The SDE method returns the normalized transition function $G(E, E_0)$ between an initial energy $E_0$ at the boundary $r_p$ and a final energy $E$ at the Earth's position. The near-Earth phase space density $f(E)$ is therefore given by: $$
f(E) = \int G(E, E_0) f^{\text{LIS}}(E_0) dE_0, \quad (10)
$$ where $f^{\text{LIS}}(E_0)$ the space density corresponding to the LIS flux $J^{\text{LIS}}(E_0)$. The integration of the equations, in practice, requires the simulation of a large number of pseudo-trajectories. An example of two typical trajectories is illustrated in Fig. 2 where the radial and colatitudinal coordinates are represented in a polar diagram. The figure shows the brownian motion of 1 GeV protons traveling from the heliopause (placed at $r = 120$ AU) to the Earth's vicinity ($r = 1$ AU). Our IMF model is azimuthally symmetric. The two trajectories are related to opposite situations of IMF polarity that will be discussed in Sect. IV. To efficiently sample the steady-state solution in the Earth's vicinity, the SDE generated trajectories were propagated backward in time, starting from Earth and until they to the heliospheric boundary [17, 27, 64]. For each pseudo-particle $k$, the method utilizes a time-step incremental scheme, $t_i^k = t_{i-1}^k + \delta t_i$, and we can determine the total duration of the trajectory as $\tau^k \equiv \sum_i \delta t_i^k$. Such a trajectory duration, calculated from the particle source to the observational point, is simply called propagation time. With a large number $N$ of simulated trajectories, the expectation value of the propagation time can be calculated as: $$
\langle \tau \rangle = \frac{\int_{0}^{\infty} t f(E, r, t) dt}{\int_{0}^{\infty} f(E, r, t) dt} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^{N} \tau^k N^k, \quad (11)
$$ where $N^k$ is the number of pseudo-particles for which the trajectory time falls in a bin around $\tau^k$. In some papers, propagation time or its expectation value are called residence time of CR in the heliosphere. It is important to note, however, that the quantity $\langle \tau \rangle$ is calculated specifically for those CR trajectories that reach Earth's position. The kinetic energy loss $E_k$ associated to a trajectory can be computed in a similar way, together with its expectation value $\langle E \rangle$. Since energy changes account only for adiabatic cooling, the simulated CR particles always end with a net energy loss: $\Delta E_k = E_0 - E_k > 0$. It should also be noted, however, that the backward propagation scheme leads to an increase of the pseudo-particle <!-- page 5 -->
energy during the simulation. This is simply due to the time-reversed adiabatic processes. In the following we will refer to the energy loss fraction $\varepsilon \equiv \Delta E_k/E_0$ and its expectation value $\langle \varepsilon \rangle$. For a given pseudo-proton trajectory, the loss fraction is calculated relatively to the proton initial energy $E_0$. The SDE method is well suited to calculate $\tau$ and $\varepsilon$. Its applicability is known since its first formulations [64, 67]. As we will discuss in Sect. IV, propagation times and energy losses of CRs depend on several factors related to the conditions of the background plasma and to the particle properties. ## B. Modeling the time dependence In our framework, near-Earth CR fluxes are calculated in terms of a time series of steady-state solutions of Eq. 1, with a resulting proton flux $J_p(t, E)$ associated with a time series of input parameters $\vec{q} = \vec{q}(t)$. The input parameters can be divided in two classes. On one side, the heliospheric parameters that characterize the variable conditions of the Sun and the surrounding plasma, i.e., the background medium where the CR propagation takes place. On the other side, the transport parameters that describe the physical processes of CR propagation through the heliosphere. In our model, we have identified a basic set of six time-dependent parameters that best capture the CR modulation phenomenon [16]. The heliospheric parameters are: the tilt angle of the heliospheric current sheet $\alpha = \alpha(t)$, the intensity of the local IMF $B_0 = B_0(t)$, and its polarity $A = A(t)$. The transport parameters are: the normalization coefficient of the parallel diffusion tensor $K_0 = K_0(t)$, and the two spectral indices $a = a(t)$ and $b = b(t)$, describing the rigidity dependence of CR diffusion below and above the break $R_k$, as seen in Eq. 5. For convenience, all parameters are expressed here as continuous functions of time $t$. In practice, their value has been evaluated from observations and eventually interpolated in defined time-grid of epochs. ## C. Determination of the heliospheric parameters The temporal dependence of the heliospheric parameters $\{\alpha, B_0, A\}$ is determined from observations. Time-series of tilt angle and polarity are continuously provided by the Wilcox Solar Observatory on 10-day or 27-day basis, respectively. Measurements of the local IMF $B_0$ are done in-situ on daily basis by spacecraft WIND and ACE on L1 orbit [44]. From these data, we build smoothed and continuous functions of time $\alpha(t)$, $B_0(t)$ and $A(t)$ by following the procedure of Fiandrini et al. [16], but with a wider time coverage. The method is based on the calculation of the backward moving average over a moving interval $[t - \tau, t]$. The extent of the interval $\tau$ ranges between 8 and 16 months, depending on the angular profile of $V_{sw}$ at a given epoch. For the tilt angle $\alpha$ a 16-month interval is used, because the current sheet lies entirely within the slow wind region, while for $B_0$ it depends on the latitudinal profile of the wind speed at a given epoch. The results are shown in Fig. 3 between 1993 and 2018. In the figure, the backward moving average functions are shown as tick solid lines, along with the measurements. We note that the considered time range spans over two solar cycles. It includes the magnetic reversal of cycle 23, when polarity changed from $A > 0$ to $A < 0$, and the latest reversal of cycle 24, where polarity changed from $A < 0$ to $A > 0$. Note that, from the figure, the polarity $A$ is given by the sign of the N/S averaged and polar field, i.e., the pink line of panel (iii). ## D. Once particles escape, they propagate in the unperturbed solar wind, which is much less magnetically turbulent compared to the shock complex region. Consequently, we assume the particles experience only weak scattering as they propagate. Because $\kappa_r$ and $U'_{\text{up}}$ both depend on $\phi$, $l_{\text{esc}}$ is also $\phi$ dependent. Furthermore, since $\kappa_r$ is energy dependent, so is $l_{\text{esc}}$. We note that $l_{\text{esc}}$ is much smaller than 1 AU ($\sim 10^{-2}$ AU for $T = 100$ MeV). The transport of energetic particles is described by the focused transport equation (FTE) (Skilling, 1971; Isenberg, 1997), with an extra term that describes cross-field diffusion $$
\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + (u_i + v\mu b_i) \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} &+ \left[ \frac{1-3\mu^2}{2} b_i b_j \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} - \frac{1-\mu^2}{2} \frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i} - \frac{\mu b_i}{v} \left( \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial t} + u_i \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} \right) \right] v \frac{\partial f}{\partial v} \\ &+ \frac{1-\mu^2}{2} \left[ v \frac{\partial b_i}{\partial x_i} + \mu \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_i} - 3\mu b_i b_j \frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i} - \frac{2b_i}{v} \left( \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial t} + u_j \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} \right) \right] \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mu} = \\ &\nabla \cdot (\kappa_{\perp} \cdot \nabla f) + \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} D_{\mu\mu} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mu} + S - L. \end{aligned} \qquad (18)
$$ <!-- page 10 -->
In equation (18), the $b_i$ and $u_i$ are the components of the unit magnetic field and solar wind speed; $\mu$ is the cosine of the particle pitch angle. $S$ and $L$ are source and loss terms, and $\nabla \cdot (\kappa_{\perp} \cdot \nabla f)$ is the term that describes the cross-field diffusion (Dröge et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2009). Except for the perpendicular diffusion term, equation (18) is the standard form of the mixed coordinate gyrophase-averaged form of the transport equation, that is, boosted into the background flow frame (here the solar wind frame). A complete derivation of equation (18) can be found in the book by Zank (2014) (see also le Roux & Webb, 2009). The equation is written in a completely general form, and for our application, a number of the terms will be zero. Specifically, the flow velocity acceleration ($\partial u_i / \partial t$), the inertial ($u_j \partial u_i / \partial x_j$), and the shear terms ($\partial u_i / \partial x_j$) all disappear leaving only the flow velocity divergence terms. The velocity divergence scales as $U/r$ where $r$ is heliocentric distance. Similarly, gradients in the magnetic field direction term $b_i$ are present and the radial term is important close to the Sun before being dominated by the azimuthal component at larger distances. These terms introduce focusing of the particle distribution, especially closer to the Sun where the field is larger with larger gradients. The perpendicular diffusion term is not derived but introduced, which reflects not particle pitch angle scattering but the diffusion of particles due to the random walk of magnetic field lines as particles diffuse along the field. This is the basis of the NLGC theory. In this work we use a backward stochastic differential equation approach to obtain steady state solutions of the FTE. Use of a backward stochastic differential equation method to calculate spectra of solar energetic particles in SEP events has been done by many authors (e.g., Dröge et al., 2014; Wang & Qin 2015; Zhang 1999; Zhao, Zhang, et al., 2016). We follow a procedure similar to Li, Webb, et al., (2009). In order to obtain the distribution function $f(p, t_s, \mu)$ of energetic particles at a position of interest (e.g., the Earth, Mars, or STEREO locations) at some time $t_s > t_0$, with a pitch angle cosine $\mu$, we consider an ensemble of paths that starts from the destination point at time $t_s$ with momentum $p$ and pitch angle cosine $\mu$. We track each single particle's motion backward in time until it encounters the shock front with a final state $(r', p', \phi')$. We then assign a probability of each path to be the distribution function upstream of the shock $f_{\text{up}}(r', p', \phi')$ where $f_{\text{up}}(r', p', \phi')$ is obtained from the acceleration module of the model. Finally, we obtain $f(p, t_s, \mu) = \langle f_{\text{up}}(r', p', \phi') \rangle$, where the bracket denotes the ensemble average over all paths. By choosing a series of different $p_i$ and $\mu_i$ and repeating the above procedure, we can obtain the full particle distribution function $f(p, \mu, t_s)$. The above procedure can also be viewed from a Green's function approach in which solving equation (18) is achieved by obtaining the convolution of Green's function $G(r', p', \phi'; p, t_s)$ with the spectrum at the shock front through (Gleeson & Webb, 1980): $$
f(p, \mu, t_s) = \int G(r', p', \phi'; p, \mu, t_s) f_{\text{up}}(r', p', \phi') dp'. \quad (19)
$$ One advantage of using a backward Kolmogorov's equation approach is that it can be easily programed numerically using a Monte Carlo code. Since a Monte Carlo code is very parallel-computing friendly, the transport module of the iPATH model can be very efficient time wise, as long as enough computational resources (nodes) are available. Due to the inclusion of cross-field diffusion, particles that escape from the shock front at the same temporal and spatial location will have been scattered on to a wide longitudinal range of field lines when reaching 1 AU. Similarly, particles arriving at 1 AU at the same time can leave the shock front from a broad radial and longitudinal range. In following a single particle's motion, we update its momentum $p$, heliocentric distance $r$, pitch angle cosine $\mu$, and longitude $\phi$ after each time step $\delta t = -30(\frac{r}{1 \text{ AU}})^{1.5} (\text{s})$. This consists of three main steps: (1) updating $(r, p, \mu, \phi)$ from the streaming, the adiabatic deceleration effect and pitch angle focusing using a RK4 scheme; (2) updating $\mu$ due to pitch angle diffusion; and (3) updating particle location $(r, \phi)$ due to perpendicular diffusion. The formalism of the pitch angle scattering is developed in the solar wind frame since pitch angle scattering is a local effect. We use the solar wind frame as the reference frame in our code. In a Parker field, the adiabatic cooling and the effect of pitch angle focusing along the IMF can be treated analytically with expressions (Ruffolo, 1995): $$
\begin{aligned} \dot{p} &= -p u_{\text{sw}} \left[ \frac{\sec \psi}{2L(z)} (1 - \mu^2) + \cos \psi \frac{d}{dr} \sec \psi \mu^2 \right] \\ \dot{\mu} &= \frac{v}{2L(z)} \left[ 1 + \mu \frac{u_{\text{sw}}}{v} \sec \psi - \mu \frac{u_{\text{sw}} v}{c^2} \sec \psi \right] (1 - \mu^2) - u_{\text{sw}} \left( \cos \psi \frac{d}{dr} \sec \psi \right) \mu (1 - \mu^2), \end{aligned} \quad (20)
$$ <!-- page 11 -->
where $\psi$ is the angle between the radial direction and the (outward pointing) magnetic field direction, $L(z)$ is the scale length of the interplanetary magnetic field (Roelof, 1969), and $z$ is the arc length from the Sun along the magnetic field. We have $$
\sec \psi = \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\Omega_{\odot}}{u_{\text{sw}}} \right)^2 r^2}; \qquad (21)
$$ $$
\frac{1}{L(z)} \equiv -\frac{1}{B(z)} \frac{\partial B(z)}{z}. $$ To update a particle's state variable $(r, p, \mu, \phi)$ in the first step, we use an RK4 scheme to solve the first-order differential equations $$
\begin{aligned} dz &= v\mu\delta t; & dr &= dz / \sec(\psi); \\ dp &= \dot{p}\delta t; & d\mu &= \dot{\mu}\delta t. \end{aligned} \qquad (22)
$$ Note that there is a one to one correspondence between $\phi$ and $r$ for a Parker spiral magnetic field. Since particles do not jump between field lines in this step, we obtain $\phi$ from $r$ directly after we update $r$. In the second step, we consider the change of pitch angle due to pitch angle diffusion. Following Zhao and Li (2014), the change in pitch angle $\delta\mu$ in this step is given by $$
\delta\mu' = \text{sign} \left( \epsilon' - \frac{1}{2} \right) \text{erf}^{-1}(\epsilon) \sqrt{4D_{\mu\mu}|\delta t|} + \frac{\partial D_{\mu\mu}}{\partial \mu} \delta t, \qquad (23)
$$ where $\text{erf}^{-1}$ is the inverse error function.

Implementation This section is devoted to some technical details concerning the numerical simulation of transport equation (1) by means of SDEs. ## 3.1. Random numbers The advantages of unconditioned stability and independence of a spatial grid are bought by the fact that a usually very large number of particles have to be evaluated at each point of interest in the 5D $(\vec{r}, q, t)$ domain. In contrast to traditional, i.e. deterministic, numerical approaches with finite-difference or finite-volume methods, SDEs contain the random part (Eq. (3)). Because random numbers are needed for a large number of particles and at every single time step, special attention has to be dedicated to their generation, which in numerical realisations are usually referred to as pseudo random numbers. A common method to generate equally distributed pseudo random numbers with large periods is the so-called Mersenne twister [20], which we use to generate pseudo random numbers in the range (0, 1].¹ Subsequently, the Box–Muller [21] algorithm is applied to transform two equally distributed pseudo random numbers, $R_1$ and $R_2$, provided by the Mersenne twister, into two normally distributed ones, $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$: $$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_1 &= \sqrt{-2 \ln(R_1)} \cos(2\pi R_2), \\
\eta_2 &= \sqrt{-2 \ln(R_1)} \sin(2\pi R_2),
\end{aligned} 
\quad (21)
$$ which theoretically can assume values in the entire range $(-\infty, \infty)$. From a practical point of view, this range is limited due to the internal representation of (floating-point) numbers on a machine. The largest possible value of $\eta_{1,2}$ is determined by the smallest possible value of $R_1$. Neglecting the subnormal (underflow) range these values are of the order of $10^{-38}$ ($10^{-308}$) for single (double) precision, leading to maximum values for $\eta_{1,2}$ of ~13 and ~38. The present algorithm restricts this range even more through the division by an integer number of ~$4.3 \times 10^9$, leading to $\eta_{1,2} \lesssim 6.7$, so that the numerical realisation restricts the stochastic process to finite propagation speeds. ## 3.2. Source and loss terms Traditional numerical approaches with finite-difference (or finite-volume) schemes need a spatial grid with a boundary that is restricted to more or less reflect the structure of this grid, so that, e.g. a curved boundary in a Cartesian grid requires some effort or cannot be realised at all. In case of SDEs, we are instead dealing merely with trajectories of pseudo particles, which at any time, $t_j$, are described by the actual position of the particle, where $t_j = \tau_{min} + jdt$ (time-forward integration) or $t_j = \tau_{max} - jdt$ (time-backward integration) with the (fixed) time step $dt$, where $j$ counts the time steps. This position may be expressed by a vector $Q_j = (x_j, y_j, z_j, q_j, t_j)$, which does not need to be formulated by any grid indices onto which it has to fit. Unless a boundary is encountered, the time-forward (time-backward) integration starts at $t_i = \tau_{min}$ ($\tau_{max}$) and stops at $t_f = \tau_{max}$ ($\tau_{min}$). The 4D physical domain is defined alone by its (inner and/or outer) boundary, expressed by a function $\varphi(r) = 0$, which may in general also depend on $t$.

Therefore, the data is technically consistent with the hypothetical (though perhaps, uninteresting) case where the effective transport rate is some constant value $\kappa_{\text{eff}} > 10^{31} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ s}^{-1}$ throughout the halo. However, given the apparent increasing $\kappa_{\text{eff}}^{\text{min}}$ trend in the inner CGM, the data hint at a spatially-varying cosmic-ray transport rate within the CGM. This implied qualitative trend is unsurprising since most of the known processes that drive cosmic-ray scattering² (e.g., the strength of turbulence, magnetic field amplitude, electron densities, cosmic-ray energy densities driving streaming instabilities) become weaker in the diffuse environments typically found in the CGM and intergalactic medium (see the discussion in Hopkins et al. 2021b). The quantitative constraint presented in Figure 2 is stronger, suggesting that the effective cosmic-ray transport rates rise to $\kappa_{\text{eff}} > 10^{31} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ s}^{-1}$ for $r \gtrsim 0.25 r_{\text{vir}}$. For the $L_*$ galaxies in the COS-Halos sample, this corresponds to physical distances of $r \gtrsim 50-100$ kpc from the galactic center. If other galaxies have similar cosmic-ray transport physics to those in the Milky Way ($\kappa_{\text{eff}} \sim 10^{28-29} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ s}^{-1}$ within the galactic disk; e.g., Trotta et al. 2011; Maurin 2020; De La Torre Luque et al. 2021; Hopkins et al. 2022b; Korsmeier & Cuoco 2021), then these data necessarily rule out a constant cosmic-ray transport rate between the galaxy disk and halo. As noted above, the effective cosmic-ray transport rate can arise from diffusive or streaming type behavior. The minimum effective field-parallel cosmic-ray streaming speed, correcting for geometry (from $\kappa_{\text{eff}}^{\text{min}}$ being isotropically averaged), implied by the lower-limit $\kappa_{\text{eff}} > 10^{31} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ s}^{-1}$ at $\sim 100$ kpc becomes $v_{\text{eff}}^{\text{stream}} \gtrsim 1000 \text{ km s}^{-1}$ in the outer CGM. Therefore, regardless of whether the constraint is phrased in terms of streaming speed, diffusivity, or advection with galactic outflows, we obtain robust indications that cosmic-ray transport speeds increase in the halo and outer CGM compared to standard ISM values. # 5. CONCLUSIONS We present a simple analytic model that provides a robust lower limit to the effective cosmic-ray transport rate for the $\sim 1-10$ GeV protons that dominate the cosmic-ray energy density and pressure in the circumgalactic and intergalactic medium (CGM/IGM), where thus far almost no observational constraints exist. Such constraints are of profound importance, not only for informing models of cosmic-ray transport themselves, but also for models of how cosmic rays influence galaxy formation through, e.g., the generation of galactic winds, cooling flows, and the phase structure of the CGM/IGM. We demonstrate that as long as a non-negligible fraction of cosmic rays escape the galactic disk, then we can estimate a minimum effective cosmic-ray transport rate, $\kappa_{\text{eff}}^{\text{min}}$, that is a function of three observed quantities: the galaxy star-formation rate ($\dot{M}_*$; ideally averaged over relatively long timescales), the circular velocity ($V_c(r)$), and the total hydrogen column density ($N_{\text{H}}$). We note that $\kappa_{\text{eff}}^{\text{min}}$ describes the total effective cosmic-ray transport rate, not only the transport rate relative to the gas, and is agnostic to the cosmic-ray transport model (e.g., diffusion, streaming, or advection). We validate this relation and the underlying assumptions using a suite of simulated galaxies with a range of masses and cosmic-ray transport physics, all calibrated to reproduce existing cosmic-ray observational constraints. Although some of these simulations have CGM that are dominated by cosmic-ray pressure and others have halos with negligibly small cosmic-ray pressures, all validate our method as a robust lower limit. We also show the lower limit remains a valid lower limit even if other sources of cosmic rays (e.g. from AGN or structure formation shocks) dominate. We caution against application to extreme starburst galaxies like Arp 220, where cosmic-ray protons suffer significant losses in the galactic disk. However, excluding these systems, we show that for dwarf-through-$\sim L_*$, star-forming galaxies at $z \lesssim 1-2$, this simple relation for $\kappa_{\text{eff}}^{\text{min}}$ (Equation 7) is a robust lower limit to the true cosmic-ray transport rate (Figure 1). We then apply our model to estimate $\kappa_{\text{eff}}^{\text{min}}$ for the star-forming COS-Halos galaxies in Figure 2. Even with large observational systematic uncertainties in the input values $N_{\text{H}}$, $V_c(r)$, and $\dot{M}_*$, the fact that there are, at present, essentially no constraints on the cosmic-ray transport coefficients for $\sim$GeV protons in the CGM/IGM means that essentially every one of these limits, even with its attendant uncertainty, is extremely interesting. We find that the resulting $\kappa_{\text{eff}}^{\text{min}}$ values strongly suggest a spatially-varying $\kappa_{\text{eff}}$ in the CGM, rising from the canonical observationally-constrained ISM values at $\lesssim 10$ kpc to values $\kappa_{\text{eff}} \gtrsim 10^{30-31} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ s}^{-1}$ ($v_{\text{eff}}^{\text{stream}} \gtrsim 1000 \text{ km s}^{-1}$) in the outer halo at galactocentric distances $\gtrsim 50-100$ kpc. The data appear to quite clearly rule out any model where the cosmic-ray transport rate is constant, with values $\kappa_{\text{eff}} \ll 10^{30} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ s}^{-1}$ in the CGM. There are, of course, more detailed physical uncertainties underpinning the assumptions made here, which could be refined with additional observational data to sharpen the constraints presented here. Physically, we do assume some cosmic-ray gas coupling so that cosmic-ray pressure could, in principle act on gas in the CGM. One might then wonder, if cosmic-ray scattering were to somehow cease in the CGM, if ² In most theoretical models, the cosmic-ray scattering rate is inversely related to the effective cosmic-ray transport rate. <!-- page 8 -->
it would render our conclusions invalid. Since the zero-scattering limit is formally equivalent to the limit where $\kappa_{\text{eff}} \to \infty$ (cosmic rays free-stream at $c$), our lower limits would remain valid lower limits. However, this limit is not expected in any reasonable physical model. Existing observational constraints on cosmic rays, including $\gamma$-ray emission, grammage, residence times, energy densities and ionization rates, all only constrain cosmic rays around the star-forming ISM (at $R \lesssim 10$ kpc). As a result, different theoretical cosmic-ray transport models can reproduce these same observations with similar $\kappa_{\text{eff}}$ in the ISM, but with $\kappa_{\text{eff}}$ diverging by up to $\sim 4$ dex in the CGM, where there are essentially no constraints at the present (at least for the typical dwarf and Milky Way-mass galaxies in the sample considered here). Thus, the proposed constraint on $\kappa_{\text{eff}}^{\text{min}}$ in the CGM presents a *qualitative* change to our ability to understand cosmic-ray microphysics and, therefore, the role cosmic rays may play in galaxy formation and plasma physics in galaxy halos. The general expression is $$
\kappa_{\parallel} = \frac{w B^2 r_g^2}{4} \int_0^1 \frac{\mu (1 - \mu^2) d\mu}{P_{\text{slab}}(1/\mu r_g)}, \quad (3)
$$ where $r_g$ is the gyroradius, $\mu$ is pitch angle, and $P_{\text{slab}}$ is the turbulent power spectrum (of one component, $\delta B_x$ or $\delta B_y$, for the mean field along $\hat{e}_z$) in the slab component, which has all wavevectors aligned with the mean magnetic field. Calculating $\kappa_{\parallel}$ according to (3) requires knowledge the turbulent intensity and the spectral shape. The latter is commonly assumed to consist of a flat energy-containing range and a power-law inertial range. The transition between the two occurs at the inverse “bendover” length $l_b$, corresponding, approximately, to the characteristic size of large-scale eddies in the flow (Zhou and Matthaeus 1990; Zank et al. 1996). The distribution of $P_{xx}$ and $l_b$ may be obtained using a model of turbulent transport (e.g., Breech et al. 2008). <!-- page 6 -->
A theory of perpendicular diffusion must take into account fluctuations that are transverse to the mean magnetic field because slab turbulence merely makes the particles retrace their path due to scattering, resulting in a subdiffusive overall transport (Kota and Jokipii 2000). Diffusion is recovered when the turbulent field possesses a transverse structure in addition to a variation along the mean field (Qin et al. 2002). Several expressions for $\kappa_{\perp}$ that take this into account in some way are in use in the simulation community, two of the more common being a phenomenological expression $\kappa_{\perp} \sim \kappa_{\parallel}$ (e.g., le Roux et al. 1999), and a more rigorously justified nonlinear guiding center (NLGC) expression where $\kappa_{\perp}$ and $\kappa_{\parallel}$ both enter into a nonlinear equation (Matthaeus et al. 2003; Zank et al. 2004; Shalchi et al. 2004). In both cases the ratio $\kappa_{\perp}/\kappa_{\parallel}$ depends critically on the power in the so-called two-dimensional (2D) turbulence with wavevectors orthogonal to the mean magnetic field (Matthaeus et al. 1990; Bieber et al. 1996). Interplanetary turbulence is highly anisotropic with 80% of the total power residing in the 2D component and 20% in the slab component. The NLGC expression for $\kappa_{\perp}$ at GCR energies (10 MeV and above) is $$
\kappa_{\perp} = b \left( \frac{\langle \delta B_{2\text{D}}^2 \rangle l_b w}{B^2 3} \right)^{2/3} \kappa_{\parallel}^{1/3} . \qquad (4)
$$ Here $\langle \delta B_{2\text{D}}^2 \rangle$ is the turbulent power in the 2D component and $b$ is a constant of order one. Expressions (2)–(3) tend to produce very large drift and diffusion coefficients in the polar regions where the magnetic field is almost radial. These large transport coefficients are often incompatible with the observed GCR intensities in the inner heliosphere. For this reason a small transverse magnetic field component is added to the Parker field background as prescribed by Jokipii and Kota (1989) or Smith and Bieber (1991). # 3 Modeling Strategies The authors of this review represent two different schools of thought on cosmic ray modeling. Generally, theoretical or empirical parameters and boundary conditions are fed into a computer model to produce a result that could explain an observation and provide a feedback for the theory. The first approach, followed by one of the authors, steers closer to the theoretical side and attempts to model the GCR process from first principles. This means using an MHD model-based input and turbulence/diffusion model that is more closely related to a theory. The approach is not devoid from free parameters, which include the turbulent intensity at the lower boundary, the correlation length, and the magnitude of the modified polar magnetic field. It is usually more difficult to obtain a good fit to observations using this more theoretical approach. The second approach is more empirical. Here a large number of parameters are utilized to fine-tune model diffusion and drift coefficients. In addition, the background flow is usually prescribed, rather than modeled. In this approach good fits to multiple observations could be obtained. These more empirical models provide useful feedback on the validity of the various assumptions that follow from the theory. The transport (1) is solved on a computer using either (a) a grid-based (“field”) or (b) a stochastic trajectory (“particle”) approach. The “field” regards the phase space distribution of energetic particles $f(\mathbf{r}, p)$ as a four-dimensional scalar field, discretized on an appropriate numerical grid. Numerical integration of the parabolic Parker equation requires an implicit solver because of the dominant diffusive term. # 7.5 EP Algorithm Benchmarks We now benchmark the EP algorithm, which constitutes the architectural core of this work. While the P-FFA pipeline addresses low-dimensional parameter spaces through structured grid evaluation, the EP framework is designed to avoid exhaustive enumeration in high-dimensional searches ( $k_{max} \geq 2$ ). For consistency with the P-FFA benchmarks, all EP benchmarks adopt the same baseline profile configuration introduced in Section 7.4: $b_{min} = 32$ , $b_{max} = 1024$ , and g = 1.5. For each configuration, we measure the explicit execution time for a single representative frequency chunk centred at a spin frequency of f = 333 Hz. This runtime is then scaled linearly to the full search range, $f \in [1, 500]$ Hz, using the number of sequential frequency blocks required to maintain the folded-profile bin resolution described in Section 7.1. Since the sequential block pipeline can be further optimized through improved memory saturation and chunk-wise targeted thresholding, the scaled runtimes reported here should be regarded as conservative upper-bound estimates of the computational cost. To characterize performance across a broad range of workloads, we sweep time-series lengths spanning 5–72 min together with a range of $\eta$ values, matching the P-FFA benchmarks.

Interpretability of data Occasionally, DL techniques are analyzed to act as a black box. In fact, they are interpretable. The need for a method of interpreting DL, which is used to obtain the valuable motifs and patterns recognized by the network, is common in many fields, such as bioinformatics [167]. In the task of disease diagnosis, it is not only required to know the disease diagnosis or prediction results of a trained DL model, but also how to enhance the surety of the prediction outcomes, as the model makes its decisions based on these verifications [168]. To achieve this, it is possible to give a score of importance for every <!-- page 47 -->

In the perturbation-based approaches, a portion of the input is changed and the effect of this change on the model output is observed [170–173]. This concept has high computational complexity, but it is simple to understand. On the other hand, to check the score of the importance of various input portions, the signal from the output propagates back to the input layer in the back-propagation-based techniques. These techniques have been proven valuable in [174]. In different scenarios, various meanings can represent the model interpretability. Uncertainty scaling Commonly, the final prediction label is not the only label required when employing DL techniques to achieve the prediction; the score of confidence for every inquiry from the model is also desired. The score of confidence is defined as how confident the model is in its prediction [175]. Since the score of confidence prevents belief in unreliable and misleading predictions, it is a significant attribute, regardless of the application scenario. In biology, the confidence score reduces the resources and time expended in proving the outcomes of the misleading prediction. Generally speaking, in healthcare or similar applications, the uncertainty scaling is frequently very significant; it helps in evaluating automated clinical decisions and the reliability of machine learning-based disease-diagnosis [176, 177]. Because overconfident prediction can be the output of different DL models, the score of probability (achieved from the softmax output of the direct-DL) is often not in the correct scale [178]. Note that the softmax output requires post-scaling to achieve a reliable probability score. For outputting the probability score in the correct scale, several techniques have been introduced, including Bayesian Binning into Quantiles (BBQ) [179], isotonic regression [180], histogram binning [181], and the legendary Platt scaling [182]. More specifically, for DL techniques, temperature scaling was recently introduced, which achieves superior performance compared to the other techniques. Catastrophic forgetting This is defined as incorporating new information into a plain DL model, made possible by interfering with the learned information. For instance, consider a case where there are 1000 types of flowers and a model is trained to classify these flowers, after which a new type of flower is introduced; if the model is fine-tuned only with this new class, its performance will become unsuccessful with the older classes [183, 184]. The logical data are continually collected and renewed, which is in fact a highly typical scenario in many fields, e.g. Biology. To address this issue, there is a direct solution that involves employing old and new data to train an entirely new model from scratch. This solution is time-consuming and computationally intensive; furthermore, it leads to an unstable state for the learned representation of the initial data. At this time, three different types of ML techniques, which have not catastrophic forgetting, are made available to solve the human brain problem founded on the neurophysiological theories [185, 186]. Techniques of the first type are founded on regularizations such as EWC [183] Techniques of the second type employ rehearsal training techniques and dynamic neural network <!-- page 48 -->
architecture like iCaRL [187, 188]. Finally, techniques of the third type are founded on dual-memory learning systems [189]. Refer to [190–192] in order to gain more details. ## Model compression To obtain well-trained models that can still be employed productively, DL models have intensive memory and computational requirements due to their huge complexity and large numbers of parameters [193, 194]. One of the fields that is characterized as data-intensive is the field of healthcare and environmental science. These needs reduce the deployment of DL in limited computational-power machines, mainly in the healthcare field. The numerous methods of assessing human health and the data heterogeneity have become far more complicated and vastly larger in size [195]; thus, the issue requires additional computation [196]. Furthermore, novel hardware-based parallel processing solutions such as FPGAs and GPUs [197–199] have been developed to solve the computation issues associated with DL. Recently, numerous techniques for compressing the DL models, designed to decrease the computational issues of the models from the starting point, have also been introduced. These techniques can be classified into four classes. In the first class, the redundant parameters (which have no significant impact on model performance) are reduced. This class, which includes the famous deep compression method, is called parameter pruning [200]. In the second class, the larger model uses its distilled knowledge to train a more compact model; thus, it is called knowledge distillation [201, 202]. In the third class, compact convolution filters are used to reduce the number of parameters [203]. In the final class, the information parameters are estimated for preservation using low-rank factorization [204]. For model compression, these classes represent the most representative techniques. In [193], it has been provided a more comprehensive discussion about the topic. ## Overfitting DL models have excessively high possibilities of resulting in data overfitting at the training stage due to the vast number of parameters involved, which are correlated in a complex manner. Such situations reduce the model's ability to achieve good performance on the tested data [90, 205]. This problem is not only limited to a specific field, but involves different tasks. Therefore, when proposing DL techniques, this problem should be fully considered and accurately handled. In DL, the implied bias of the training process enables the model to overcome crucial overfitting problems, as recent studies suggest [205–208]. Even so, it is still necessary to develop techniques that handle the overfitting problem. An investigation of the available DL algorithms that ease the overfitting problem can categorize them into three classes. The first class acts on both the model architecture and model parameters and includes the most familiar approaches, such as weight decay [209], batch normalization [210], and dropout [90]. In DL, the default technique is weight decay [209], which is used extensively in almost all ML algorithms as a universal regularizer. The second class works on model inputs such as data corruption and data augmentation [150, 211]. One reason for the overfitting problem is the lack of training data, which makes the learned distribution not mirror the real distribution. Data augmentation enlarges the training data. By contrast, marginalized data corruption improves the solution exclusive to augmenting the data. The final class works on the <!-- page 49 -->
model output. A recently proposed technique penalizes the over-confident outputs for regularizing the model [178]. This technique has demonstrated the ability to regularize RNNs and CNNs. ## Vanishing gradient problem In general, when using backpropagation and gradient-based learning techniques along with ANNs, largely in the training stage, a problem called the vanishing gradient problem arises [212–214]. More specifically, in each training iteration, every weight of the neural network is updated based on the current weight and is proportionally relative to the partial derivative of the error function. However, this weight updating may not occur in some cases due to a vanishingly small gradient, which in the worst case means that no extra training is possible and the neural network will stop completely. Conversely, similarly to other activation functions, the sigmoid function shrinks a large input space to a tiny input space. Thus, the derivative of the sigmoid function will be small due to large variation at the input that produces a small variation at the output. In a shallow network, only some layers use these activations, which is not a significant issue. While using more layers will lead the gradient to become very small in the training stage, in this case, the network works efficiently. The back-propagation technique is used to determine the gradients of the neural networks. Initially, this technique determines the network derivatives of each layer in the reverse direction, starting from the last layer and progressing back to the first layer. The next step involves multiplying the derivatives of each layer down the network in a similar manner to the first step. For instance, multiplying N small derivatives together when there are N hidden layers employs an activation function such as the sigmoid function. Hence, the gradient declines exponentially while propagating back to the first layer. More specifically, the biases and weights of the first layers cannot be updated efficiently during the training stage because the gradient is small. Moreover, this condition decreases the overall network accuracy, as these first layers are frequently critical to recognizing the essential elements of the input data. However, such a problem can be avoided through employing activation functions. These functions lack the squishing property, i.e., the ability to squish the input space to within a small space. By mapping X to max, the ReLU [91] is the most popular selection, as it does not yield a small derivative that is employed in the field. Another solution involves employing the batch normalization layer [81]. As mentioned earlier, the problem occurs once a large input space is squashed into a small space, leading to vanishing the derivative. Employing batch normalization degrades this issue by simply normalizing the input, i.e., the expression $|x|$ does not accomplish the exterior boundaries of the sigmoid function. The normalization process makes the largest part of it come down in the green area, which ensures that the derivative is large enough for further actions. Furthermore, faster hardware can tackle the previous issue, e.g. that provided by GPUs. This makes standard back-propagation possible for many deeper layers of the network compared to the time required to recognize the vanishing gradient problem [215]. <!-- page 50 -->
## Exploding gradient problem Opposite to the vanishing problem is the one related to gradient. Specifically, large error gradients are accumulated during back-propagation [216–218]. The latter will lead to extremely significant updates to the weights of the network, meaning that the system becomes unsteady. Thus, the model will lose its ability to learn effectively. Grosso modo, moving backward in the network during back-propagation, the gradient grows exponentially by repetitively multiplying gradients.

Here, we focus on the PINN for hyperelasticity (specifically, incompressible Neo-Hookean material) as most of our computational examples adopt this material model (see section S2 for the mechanics of hyperelastic materials). To better clarify the quantitative formulation, here, we denote all the material and geometric parameters of interest as $\theta_{\text{mat}}$ and $\theta_{\text{geo}}$, respectively. For incompressible Neo-Hookean materials, the only material parameter is the shear modulus $\mu$ so that $\theta_{\text{mat}} = \mu$. The unknown part of $\theta = (\theta_{\text{mat}}, \theta_{\text{geo}})$ in the inverse problem is denoted as $\theta_{\text{unk}}$. As summarized in Results, the workflow of PINNs comprises four steps. First, we apply a NN to approximate the primary solution fields (top left panel in Fig. 2B) in domain $\Omega(\theta_{\text{geo}})$, including the displacement field $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda)$ and the pressure field $\tilde{\mathbf{p}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda)$, where $\lambda$ represents trainable parameters of the NN, $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2)$ is the in-plane coordinates in the reference/undeformed configuration, and the quantities with tilde represent the approximation from the NN. For incompressible materials, we need the hydrostatic pressure field $p$ as a Lagrange multiplier accompanying the displacement field $\mathbf{u}$ to uniquely determine the stress field. Second, we integrate mechanical laws into the PINN architecture (top right panel in Fig. 2B) by deriving relevant mechanical quantities of interest from the NN outputs. During this calculation process, partial derivatives are handled by automatic differentiation. The deformation gradient $\tilde{\mathbf{F}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda)$ and the first Piola-Kirchhoff stress $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda, \mu)$ are calculated by $$
\tilde{\mathbf{F}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda) = \mathbf{I} + \frac{\partial \tilde{\mathbf{u}}}{\partial \mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda) \quad (4)
$$ $$
\tilde{\mathbf{P}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda, \mu) = -\tilde{\mathbf{p}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda) \tilde{\mathbf{F}}^{-T}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda) + \mu \tilde{\mathbf{F}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda) \quad (5)
$$ where $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity tensor, Eq. 4 is kinematics, and Eq. 5 is the constitutive relation for incompressible Neo-Hookean materials. The residuals of the equilibrium PDE and the incompressibility condition at $\mathbf{X}$ are expressed by $$
\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\text{PDE}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda, \mu) = \text{Div} \, \tilde{\mathbf{P}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda, \mu), \quad \mathbf{X} \in \Omega(\theta_{\text{geo}}) \quad (6)
$$ $$
\tilde{r}_{\text{inc}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda) = \det(\tilde{\mathbf{F}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda)) - 1, \quad \mathbf{X} \in \Omega(\theta_{\text{geo}}) \quad (7)
$$ The residuals of Dirichlet/displacement and Neumann/traction BCs at $\mathbf{X}$ are $$
\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\text{D}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda) = \tilde{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda) - \bar{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{X}), \quad \mathbf{X} \in \partial \Omega_{\text{D}}(\theta_{\text{geo}}) \quad (8)
$$ $$
\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\text{N}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda, \mu) = \tilde{\mathbf{P}}(\mathbf{X}; \lambda, \mu) \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{X}) - \bar{\mathbf{T}}(\mathbf{X}), \quad \mathbf{X} \in \partial \Omega_{\text{N}}(\theta_{\text{geo}}) \quad (9)
$$ where $\mathbf{N}$ is the outward unit normal vector on the boundary, and $\bar{\mathbf{u}}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{T}}$ are the specified displacement and traction on the boundary, respectively. $\partial \Omega_{\text{D}}(\theta_{\text{geo}})$ and $\partial \Omega_{\text{N}}(\theta_{\text{geo}})$ refer to the domains for Dirichlet/displacement and Neumann/traction BCs, respectively. For inverse problems, we have displacement data $\{\mathbf{u}^{*(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_u}$ at $\{\mathbf{X}_u^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_u}$. The residual of the $i$th displacement observation is $$
\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{(i)}(\lambda) = \tilde{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{X}_{u}^{(i)}; \lambda) - \mathbf{u}^{*(i)} \quad (10)
$$ Third, we formulate the loss function according to the foregoing residuals from mechanics and data (bottom right panel in Fig. 2B). To define the loss terms corresponding to the problem definition, we place $N_{\Omega}$, $N_{\text{D}}$, and $N_{\text{N}}$ residual points in $\Omega$, on $\partial \Omega_{\text{D}}$ and $\partial \Omega_{\text{N}}$, denoted as $\mathbf{X}_{\Omega}^{(i)}$ ($i \in \{1, 2, \dots, N_{\Omega}\}$), $\mathbf{X}_{\text{D}}^{(i)}$ ($i \in \{1, 2, \dots, N_{\text{D}}\}$), and $\mathbf{X}_{\text{N}}^{(i)}$ ($i \in \{1, 2, \dots, N_{\text{N}}\}$), respectively. Because we parameterize the coordinates of residual points by $\theta_{\text{geo}}$, these residual points are all parameterized by $\theta_{\text{geo}}$. We evaluate the mean squared residuals of the PDEs, the incompressibility condition, Dirichlet and Neumann BCs, and data, respectively. Each loss term is defined by $$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE}}(\lambda, \theta) = \frac{1}{N_{\Omega}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\Omega}} |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\text{PDE}}(\mathbf{X}_{\Omega}^{(i)}(\theta_{\text{geo}}); \lambda, \mu)|^2 \quad (11)
$$ $$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{inc}}(\lambda, \theta) = \frac{1}{N_{\Omega}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\Omega}} |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\text{inc}}(\mathbf{X}_{\Omega}^{(i)}(\theta_{\text{geo}}); \lambda)|^2 \quad (12)
$$ $$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{D}}(\lambda, \theta) = \frac{1}{N_{\text{D}}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{D}}} |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_{\text{D}}(\mathbf{X}_{\text{D}}^{(i)}(\theta_{\text{geo}}); \lambda)|^2 \quad (13)
$$

\vec{\kappa} = \begin{pmatrix} \kappa_{\perp} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \kappa_{\perp} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \kappa_{\parallel} \end{pmatrix} . \qquad (6)
$$ In our simulation, the diffusion tensor can be transferred to our spherical coordinates using the following form: $$
\vec{\kappa} = \begin{pmatrix} \kappa_{\perp} \cos^2 \psi + \sin^2 \psi \kappa_{\parallel} & 0 & -\cos \psi \sin \psi \kappa_{\perp} + \sin \psi \cos \psi \kappa_{\parallel} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin \psi \cos \psi \kappa_{\perp} + \cos \psi \sin \psi \kappa_{\parallel} & 0 & \sin^2 \psi \kappa_{\perp} + \cos^2 \psi \kappa_{\parallel} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad (7)
$$ where $\psi$ is the angle between the local magnetic field direction $\mathbf{B}$ and the radial direction $\mathbf{r}$. Transformations to other coordinate systems can be done in a similar manner. For the diffusion coefficient, we choose the following general form: $$
\kappa_{\parallel} = \kappa_{\parallel 0} \beta \left( \frac{p}{p_0} \right)^{b_{\parallel}} \left( \frac{B_{\text{eq}}}{B} \right)^{a_{\parallel}}, \qquad (8a)
$$ $$
\kappa_{\perp} = \kappa_{\perp 0} \beta \left( \frac{p}{p_0} \right)^{b_{\perp}} \left( \frac{B_{\text{eq}}}{B} \right)^{a_{\perp}}, \qquad (8b)
$$ where $p$ and $B$ are the particle momentum and magnetic field strength, respectively, and $\beta$ is the ratio of particle speed to the speed of light. The $p_0$ parameter is a reference momentum (in our case 1 GeV $c^{-1}$), $B_{\text{eq}}$ is the IMF strength at the heliospheric equator at 1 AU. The constants $\kappa_{\parallel 0}$ and $\kappa_{\perp 0}$ determine the magnitudes of parallel and perpendicular diffusion coefficients. They are chosen to be $50 \times 10^{20} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ s}^{-1}$ and $5 \times 10^{20} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ s}^{-1}$, respectively. The exponents are chosen as $a_{\parallel, \perp} = 0.5$ and $b_{\parallel, \perp} = 1$. The choice of the above diffusion coefficients is a little arbitrary, but it is approximately consistent with the overall modulation level inferred by various observations and a few other simulations of cosmic-ray modulation. V_d = \frac{pv}{3q} \nabla \times \frac{\mathbf{B}}{B^2} . $$ Both the diffusion coefficient and drift velocity are functions of magnetic field and plasma speed. $$ Here, $\Omega$ denotes the spatial domain, $\mathbf{r}_0$ the location of the injection point and $E_0$ the initial energy. Neglecting initial conditions, the general time-dependent phase-space density $f(\mathbf{r}_0, E_0, t_0)$ at any point of interest can then be calculated, in general, as (see [15]) $$
f(\mathbf{r}_0, E_0, t) = \int_S \int_{E_0}^{\infty} \int_{t_0}^{t} f_b(\mathbf{r}, E, t) \times G(\mathbf{r}, E, t|\mathbf{r}_0, E_0, t_0) dAdEdt', \quad (16)
$$ where $f_b$ is the boundary condition (e.g. the local interstellar spectrum or the Jovian electron source distribution) and the integration is performed on the surface of the boundary $S$ with the surface element $dA$. Integration in time is performed from $t_0$ to the desired time $t$, i.e. only those particles contribute to $f(\mathbf{r}_0, E_0, t)$ that reached the boundary before $t$. Note that the integration over energy starts at $E_0$, because no energies below the initial value can occur in the backward-time model if no particles acceleration occurs in the physical setup. As we are considering two species of particles, namely galactic and Jovian electrons, two disjointed boundaries are implemented in the model, such that $\Omega = \Omega_{\text{Jovian}} + \Omega_{\text{galactic}}$ ($\Omega_{\text{galactic}}$ represents the heliopause and $\Omega_{\text{Jovian}}$ the Jovian magnetosphere) with $\Omega_{\text{Jovian}} \cap \Omega_{\text{galactic}} = 0$. For a detailed discussion see [27]. ## 2.2. Advantages of SDEs Compared to finite-difference schemes, SDEs have some advantages, e.g. they are unconditionally stable. This is not the case for finite difference schemes where too large time steps may result in unstable behavior. However, the accuracy of the SDE solution is closely related to the chosen time step; smaller values of $\Delta t$ in Eq. (14) lead to more accurate results, keeping in mind that the integration scheme is only first-order accurate in $\Delta t$. Because the SDE approach has no spatial grid, the spatial resolution is governed by $\Delta t$. The time-step should be adjusted so that the simulated pseudo-particles sample the smallest spatial structure of interest. This is especially important not only for modeling shock acceleration in semi-discontinuous shocks [29], but also when small scale gradients and current sheets need to be captured [30]; for a discussion on how to vary the time step appropriately, see [31]. The set of SDEs solves the transition probability $G(\mathbf{r}, E, t|\mathbf{r}_0, E_0, t_0)$ that is independent of the boundary function, but not its position. The resulting flux is the outcome of the convolution of the transition probability with the boundary condition as shown in Eq. (16). Once a solution of a set of SDEs exists for given diffusion coefficients and drift terms and the exit times and energies (that is, the time and energy with which a pseudo-particle reaches any computational boundary) of all pseudo-particles are known, it is possible to calculate particle intensities and energy spectra for different boundary conditions (e.g. a different local interstellar spectrum) without the need to re-run the complete simulation. Thus, it is possible to calculate fluxes and energy spectra for different boundary conditions using the same transition propagation. Changing the diffusion and drift coefficients, however, requires a re-run of the algorithm since these parameters directly influence the phase-space trajectories of the pseudo-particles. In contrast to the solution of Parker's transport equation using a finite difference scheme such as the ADI (Alternating Direction Implicit) method, the solution of SDEs is less complicated. While the application of the ADI-type schemes requires the solution of a linear system of equations (including in most cases multiple matrix inversions), the solution of a SDE is simply the numerical integration of Eq. (14). Adding further terms to the Parker equation such as momentum diffusion would not increase the general level of complexity. In many cases the solution of a transport equation at a given point in space or along a planet's or spacecraft's trajectory is sufficient. While a finite difference scheme calculates the solution for the entire grid, the SDE approach allows the calculation of the fluxes and particle propagation times at one point in phase-space. Since there is no particle-particle interaction, all individual trajectories are independent. Consequently, we have a highly parallel problem that can be solved using parallel computing <!-- page 4 -->
techniques. While a finite difference solution of Parker's transport equation gives a statistical property, namely the phase space density and not the properties of real particles, the same is true for SDEs. SDEs do not solve the trajectory of a real particle or that of a test particle but rather the trajectory of a phase-space element. Consequently, the propagation of such a pseudo-particle does not directly map to the real motion of a particle that underlies the Newton-Lorentz equation. ### 3. The computing environment For our simulations we used a GeForce GTX 660 graphics card with compute capability 3.0 and 2048 MB of memory. The GPU operates at 1.10 GHz clock speed and consists of 5 multiprocessors, each of which contains 192 CUDA cores. We compiled the code using CUDA version 5.5 in combination with version 4.8.1 of the gcc compiler on Linux (Debian). We investigated the program with and without CUDA's fast math option (`use_fast_math`). The CPU version of the program was run on a i7-3770K using gcc 4.8.1. Similar to the GPU version, the program was tested with and without gcc's fast math option (`ffast_math`).
